utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you were speaking about the military line, or the Vojna Linija, in the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, and as far as I understand it, you claim that Radmilo Bogdanovic was at the head of this military line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked by the interpreters to repeat the answer which you gave, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about the military line in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another matter. In view of your position, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute -- just a moment. Let's have it formally announced.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in view of your position in the security administration, I would like to avail myself of this opportunity now that you're testifying. I would like you to confirm or deny some of the things we heard here regarding the alleged member of the KOS. That's the way he introduced himself here. His name was Slobodan Lazarevic, and the KOS is definitely an outdated thing anyway. Did I write this down properly, that you were asked here about Lazarevic, and I wrote down what you said: "Absolutely unknown. I categorically claim that he was not a member of the security of the army of Yugoslavia, rather, the JNA"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it have happened, General, that you, as head of the security administration, would not know someone who were employed by the security administration, that you would not know some security organ, at least at that level as Lazarevic introduced himself to be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is no possibility whatsoever for him to have been a member of the Kos, as he had put it and for you not to know that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Ajdinovic was mentioned, a security officer. Is it correct that it is absolutely false that in 1991, in Vojnic, the KOS organs - Ajdinovic primarily - organised the killing of two Croat brothers, the Brajic brothers from Sweden?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about this and I personally cannot believe this, that any active military personnel would be engaged in this, let alone members of the military security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ajdinovic a member of the military security?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the military security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a good officer or was he prone to crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not prone to crime. He was a good officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, he was a good officer.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had some views of his own, some problems of his own, but he was not prone to crime and I can say that basically, he was an honest officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A honest man, a honest officer. All right. Is it possible for him to carry out this kind of crime and that you did not receive any information about this whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described how the selection of information takes place. Along the vertical line of security organs, there was the possibility of this information being selected at the level of the 5th Military District security organs and that it was not sent on to me. But if something like that was in the hands of the 5th Military District, and if they did not send it up further, that would have meant concealing this kind of information. So whoever would have concealed this information would have been an accomplice in this kind of crime. However, I was a curious person, and I asked about things that happened. And when this was first mentioned, I asked around and I came to the conclusion that this was not reliable information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explanations were provided here precisely by this alleged member of the KOS that crimes were committed by the special unit of the 21st Corps under the command of Ajdinovic, inter alia, the mayor of Vrginmost, Obradovic, was killed, and further on, the Glina Vrginmost railroad was blown up and the water tower at Glina. Do you know anything about any such thing? Is there a grain of truth in any of this that was presented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... whether it's true or not. What the witness can say is whether he knew anything about it or not. What he can tell us about is his state of knowledge. Yes. Did you know anything, General, about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know anything about this, and I could not believe that Ajdinovic was commander of any kind of unit. I know that until the end of 1991 - that is to say I have reliable information about that - was in the security organs. He had various clashes with his chief, but this was within the line of work. And as far as I know, after that he left security organs. But this 21st Corps was not active when I was in the military. I think that this was a later stage. As regards the killing of Dimitrijevic [as interpreted], the president of the municipality, I would not present any indications here, but there were some indications that this was done by a different group. So there is no possibility that this was committed by Ajdinovic or any of the security officers, because this man was a communist by orientation, Obradovic, and I think that that is how he was liquidated. And all my security organs came from the same kinds of families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, it is known that this ideological confrontation was rather strained in Krajina. According to what you've been saying just now, is it clear that precisely this officer that you mentioned now could have been confronted only with the other stream that was headed by Milan Babic? I mean, not that officer, rather, the mayor of that town.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say that it was the current around Milan Babic. There were several currents over there. There were currents originating in Serbia, under the influence of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I asked you about Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on. Tell me, please, what do you know about the killing of the first security officer or, as you professionally Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. referred to him, the first security organ? I have a note here that this occurred in May or June 1991 on the road between Gorica and Zagreb, that is the airport and Zagreb, that he was a lieutenant, that he was a member of the security service, and that he was killed. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, though there were some security organs killed in Slovenia later on. He was killed at a checkpoint which was held in those days by the MUP of Croatia within the framework of an operation that they called Jez or "hedgehog." There were 12 checkpoints in several belts around Zagreb. I think that he was heading towards Sisak, if I'm not mistaken. He was on an official trip. He didn't respect the procedure, and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this lieutenant that was killed by the Croatian MUP, and he was a member of the JNA and a member of the security service, he was a Croat, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was the first member of the security service to be killed by the Croatian police in those events that started in those days?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in those days it didn't mean anything to them whether someone was a Croat or something else. The main thing for them was that he was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I have to clear up an event that you -- that is linked to Goran Radosavljevic, Gurij, his surname being Djeletovic. You claimed something about him. I don't remember whether it was in open session or in private session.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In private session. I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us say at least something in open session. General, you were saying that in the second half of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992, there were -- there was some sort of ethnic purification in the JNA of the officer cadres. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? What period did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the second half of 1991 and into 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the year 1992 and later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were talking about 1992 and later.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About a process that gained momentum and some initial pensioning off started in the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be brief. I would like to draw attention to only one matter, and that is that you said that there was ethnic purification or cleansing. I don't have many documents about this, but I do have one from the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, sector for the organisation reinforcement and information, personnel administration, the 14th of October, 1992. That was the period of time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been formed, the strength of the army had been reduced, there was reorganisation under way, and some general -- some vacancies of general posts had occurred because some had stayed in Croatia, some in Bosnia, and so on. So I'm quoting from this document because it is -- provides an explanation, and it says: "The preamble is being neglected, which clearly states that analysis of the active military officers and civilians in the army of Yugoslavia has to be done on the basis of reliability, patriotism, professionalism, and morale." So where do you see any ethnic criterion here? Professionalism, reliability, patriotism, morale. Where do you see the ethnic component? Please look at this document and tell me whether you consider it to be authentic. It was signed by Risto Matovic, the chief of department, and there's a number under which it was logged.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that absolute ethnic cleansing was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about absolute or ethnic. I'm asking you whether there was any ethnic cleansing in the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I was cautioned in my -- I don't need that. I don't need that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Would you help us, General, by having a look at it, since the accused is intending to produce it, no doubt. Just tell us what it is, whether it looks to be a genuine document or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by the form, this should be an authentic document. But it says here that certain commands, interpreting and taking measures by sector, and then there is the personnel sector, had neglected the preamble or the introductory paragraph in which these criteria were clearly specified, which means that certain commands did not comply with these criteria of reliability, patriotism, professionalism, and morale. So it means that there were certain attempts to eliminate people on the basis of other criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I am saying that from the top an intervention came containing criteria that any army in the world today respects, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can anything else -- if anything else happens, can that only be an expression of arbitrariness on the part of individuals?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in March 1992 a general holding the second most important position in the JNA --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to give the name, General Zivota Panic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was he, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, he was virtually the Chief of Staff at the time. You, young man, still have some Croats in your service. So he was referring to a captain who was working on the operation to discover weapons and the whole Spegelj affair. And he required that the security service be cleansed of those who were not Serbs or Montenegrins. And I said to him then he could then close the security administration, that he has the personnel service, and they can look at the records and see who is a Serb and who is a Montenegrin. They can stay. And I said for as long as I was head of the security service, nobody would be removed on the basis of that criterion. You mustn't smirk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me tell you why I'm smiling. Because this was a private conversation because if it had been an order you would have carried it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out. It may have been a private conversation at lunch. That is not binding on you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finish the story. First of all, I never had lunch with any one of those people or any private conversations. And when Nedeljko Boskovic came, he called out the captain by name and told him, "You go from here because your place is not here." And this man was on the payroll for many years of the security service, but he couldn't come to work. So I'm not saying that the situation throughout the army of Yugoslavia developed in that direction but that that was the intention is beyond dispute. And that is why there was this reaction. What are the criteria for the termination of employment? Not ethnicity as being a major criterion. It's not mentioned at all. But I assumed that this was the reason and that is why they're being cautioned that these criteria have to be respected; morale, patriotism, professionalism, and so on. So this indirectly corroborates what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this -- does this document show that there was an endeavour to treat people correctly regardless of their ethnicity, to treat them equally, that it has nothing to do with ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which was meant to halt a process which had already started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which could have only been an arbitrary act, because it says in individual commands such things were happening which must not happen. I'm afraid our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your time is up. Do you want that document exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. May I put two more questions only?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the document be exhibited. Bring it to the registrar. Then two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that time is running out. I do not wish to abuse your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, you mentioned that the JNA had withdrawn from Macedonia based on a meeting held between representatives of the republican authorities of Macedonia and representatives of the JNA in February 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it disputed that before the Second World War Macedonia was a part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was before the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any dispute over the fact that not a single shot was fired, nor was there any act of violence in Macedonia and that the army withdrew without any conflicts breaking out at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, though there were some minor -- minor provocations against the army in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were provocations, but nobody opened fire.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an incursion into the warehouse near Skopje where the guards were disarmed and all the weapons pulled out during the night, and we had to intervene to find where those soldiers were, and they were detained in Titov Veles. So there was a rough attack against the JNA, but there was no shooting. There was no fire. There was no spilling of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A meeting was held, and the army withdrew without a single windowpane being broken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider that that should serve as a model for the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should have been a model for the withdrawal of the JNA from any area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why, then, did a conflict occur over there? Is it true that the difference is that in Macedonia the army was not attacked whereas in these other areas very cruel and bloody attacks were made against the army? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian authority had already separated. The Serbian MUP had separated, and a separate state was being formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. This is the last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Surely you're not saying that the Serbs started the violence in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't saying that. I was saying that the difference, major difference, was in a republic in which there were large ethnic groups, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. In Croatia, Serbs and Croats. And the situation was quite different in Slovenia and Macedonia, where Serbs were very few in number and withdrawing from that area evolved much more easily and on the basis of agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've had your time. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to make an explanation to the Court first of all. I would really like to try, if I may, through my cross-examination to deal with the organisation, command and control over the Yugoslav People's Army in the context of constitutional regulations and to stick to that subject mainly. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Vasiljevic, during the examination-in-chief -- I'm sorry, this cord of my headphones is very short. I can't even stand upright. Sorry. It's fine now. You explained during the examination-in-chief that in 1987, there occurred major changes in the organisation of JNA, so you said, and that the three military districts you mentioned were set up then. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That year, apart from that organisation of these military districts, were there any other changes in the essence of the organisation, command and control over the army? I mean within the constitution.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think there were. However, part of the affairs dealing with the reinforcement and personnel of the JNA was transferred to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that these matters regarding the organisation, command and control were regulated by the constitution of 1974. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I heard, and I knew that from before, you remember that I was one of the defenders the Opera case in 1991, 1992? I don't want to use that experience in my cross-examination, and I can't use it since Mr. Nice did not ask any questions about the Opera case or Labrador, although it was in the proofing summary. I know that you were then in the service where you served and you are very well acquainted with matters regarding the issues I want to raise in my cross. I know that in 1961, you graduated from the Military Academy and that sometime in the 1970s you already had 15 years of service in the JNA in security services.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know very well about all the things that happened in the Yugoslav society, all the developments, as a man who was involved in the security service of the army, and you know what and how happened regarding the transformation command and control in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm only interested in military issues.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my job, that's all I can really answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I want to know is about military issues. You know that in those years there was a live discussion about whether the army should be professionalised and organised professionally, as in every state, and the military leadership supported this idea headed by Chief of Staff Bosnjak. This debate is still going on, but at the moment there was this other faction since self-management began to dominate in all levels of Yugoslav society. This self-management was supposed to take root even in the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an idea to socialise the army, to give a weapon to every man, to reorganise the society along the lines of arming the society and creating the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That concept existed always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was supported by Kardelj, Bakaric and Tito.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who advocated it. I know it existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the constitution of 1974 create the Territorial Defence for the first time? Was it written into the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I'm not quite certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In that way, did two parallel, equal segments of the armed forces come into being, the army and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as part of an integrated armed force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence exist then as an equal armed force of municipalities and republics?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know for certain is that it was an integral part of the armed forces, equal to the JNA but it was organised along different lines, along different principles, and I can't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did this concept, the creation of the Territorial Defence, mark a major blow to the JNA as far as command and control is concerned? I'm talking about the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such problems until the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm saying. Is it true that even back then, especially in the military leadership, there was a conviction that this is a preparation of the armed forces of the republics for providing resistance in the case of intervention by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I already said there were no problems until the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll show you later something that is written in a text, but I'm just asking you for now: Is it a fact that in 1990 and even in 1989 when the Yugoslav crisis began, there was practically in existence -- there were eight separate armies and the JNA, and the idea of withering of the state resulted in the existence of eight separate armies?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until the 1990s, I, at least, didn't notice that within the Territorial Defence there should be a separate army, alienated from the JNA, and that there was a striving to create republican armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the 1990s, after the events in Slovenia and after the creation of the Territorial Defence and armed forces in Slovenia, and that led to happening in Croatia as well, can we at least then talk about those two separate armed forces within one state.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, in Croatia that did not happen. I don't think it happened in Slovenia either. One part of the Territorial Defence was transformed and assimilated as the nucleus of a future republican army. In Croatia, the entire Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia never became the home guards corps. That's precisely why paramilitary units were formed. Therefore, the Territorial Defence did not become the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It became a separate armed force within a state which continued to exist.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continued to be the same as before, but it was undermined illegally from within. That was typical also of the events in Bosnia with the Patriotic People's League using the officers corps which was recruited for the future republican army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a broad topic. We don't have time for it. What I want to know, Mr. Vasiljevic, is the following: Can I hear from you, so the Court can understand the situation better, all that you know directly or indirectly about the functioning of the Ministry of Defence, the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, the General Staff, and especially the staff of Supreme Command in this period of 1990 until May 1992. I suppose you know this very well, taking into account the posts you held.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you specific questions. I have to stick to the examination-in-chief, to the scope of examination-in-chief, and in my cross-examination, I will be using only one document, which I received together with the indictment, and that is the text titled "State Without the Army" by Veljko Kadijevic, including some information about specific things which I suppose you knew about. You know about this writing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which part of it you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll show it to you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the book in my time. I have my own opinion about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we received this text in October 2001. It was translated into English. And as far as I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know from the Prosecution, certain data from this book need to be shown to General Vasiljevic. Would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let us recollect the position about this book. Has it been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From what document's being put, the witness must be asked whether he is prepared to deal with questions and whether he wants to deal with them in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that. Can we first of all deal with this book. I recollect references to it. I do not recollect whether it's been exhibited or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not an exhibit. If it's the Kadijevic book, we've already put it in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the Kadijevic book. Yes, I remember references to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in which case no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But there have been references to it in the evidence. General Vasiljevic, can you deal with questions about this book? You say you've read it and you've got your own opinions about it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll only be presenting certain data from this book to you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this book a long time ago, when it was published. It contains many facts which are true, according to my recollection, but there are also certain things that I never knew about and I don't think are true. It says, for instance, that the army was supposed to take over the Karlobag-Virovitica line. I never heard that from anyone from the General Staff, including General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... questions. He's going to put various passages, as I understand it, to you. Just answer them. If at any time you want to go into private session, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there is any problem that requires private session, because this is a book that was published and is known to the public. But if the need occurs, we'll deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll only deal with facts which I suppose are known to Mr. Vasiljevic, and I even think he worked on the collection of certain information that was supposed to enable these operations. I will not mention a single name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, do you know about the assessment of the staff of the Supreme Command - and I emphasise this - presented towards the end of 1989, namely the staff of the Supreme Command judged at this moment, in 1989, that control over the events in Yugoslavia is being taken over by foreign elements as well as control of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was then in the -- I was not then in the staff of the Supreme Command. I was in my division in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I'll skip all my questions. My next question is this: Do you know that on the 3rd of April, 1990, there was a session of the Presidency of the SFRY? Did you attend it, by any chance, when the staff of the Supreme Command presented certain assessments and proposals?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that at that time, to make things easier, until the 8th of July, 1990, I commanded the division in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this information ever reach you, that the staff of the Supreme Command then presented its assessment and suggested certain measures? Their assessment was as follows -- do you know about it, have you ever heard about it, or were you informed? Their assessment was that internally, the key segment of the SFRY, that is the federal system, was already broken down, the country was ruled by chaos and complete lawlessness. That's one. Second, due to the break-up of the Warsaw Pact and the events that preceded the break-up of the USSR, the Yugoslav territory became open to the West, and the West's policy towards Yugoslavia changed. Did you know about this assessment that was presented to the Presidency of the SFRY, as I said, on the 3rd of April, 1990?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, through the system of information of subordinate commands, I know about these assessments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that certain measures were suggested, primarily the reinstitution of the constitutional order and the ruling out of all enactments which are contrary to the constitution of the SFRY? Did you hear about this presented to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that according to the 1974 constitution, it is the task -- the task of the armed forces was twofold: One, defending the country from foreign aggression, and second, the protection of the constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the task of the armed forces as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that at that time the staff of the Supreme Command gave the following assessment: That the 1974 constitution ensured the destruction of the entirety, the integrity of the Yugoslav state through the constitution, while at the same time the constitution cannot be used to break up the integrity of Yugoslavia, which called for amendments of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this. I don't know whether it was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so -- I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this assessment and these proposals made by the staff of the Supreme Command of the Presidency were accepted by a majority vote?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know. And do you know whether anything that was proposed by the Supreme Command was actually put into practice?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I may assist the Court, perhaps, if I say the following: I remember that these processes of disintegration were typical of Slovenia primarily. That's where they began. Ignoring the federal constitution and disregarding about -- of about 40 laws dealing with national defence which ran counter to the constitution of Slovenia. Federal laws, that is to say there were some 40 laws from the domain of All People's Defence and self-protection that were proclaimed invalid in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come to the point why I'm putting all these questions, Mr. Vasiljevic, and I think that this will greatly assist the Court, because already in 1991, you were very active working in the Supreme Command Staff and the General Staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And towards the end of that year, the following assessment was made: The military leadership had this, and this was discussed, and this situation, in order not to improvise, I will have to read a few sentences to you from this text as an assessment and as an estimate of the military leadership, primarily the General Staff, and the Supreme Command Staff. It reads as follows: "In order to justify aggression, there were two variants. The first one, if the defenders of a united Yugoslavia were the first to apply force, then there is an excuse because, 'the Unitarian Greater Serbia forces' are trying to topple democratically elected regimes within Yugoslavia. That is the first assessment. And the second one is if this does not happen, then the secessionist forces of Yugoslavia should be compelled to use force in order to impose their own will." Are you aware of this assessment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court, to the Honourable Judges, what is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page? Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 86 and 87. I've already read that out. But what is referred to here and is put under quotation marks, this danger from the Greater Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, General Vasiljevic, in view of everything that you know about these matters, before these times, in any crisis that broke out in the territory of Yugoslavia, was it always said that it is primarily the Greater Serbian Unitarian forces that were behind that and that this was often pointed out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It depends who pointed it out. From one setting, everything that happened was always interpreted from the point of view of that particular environment. But we, in the top military echelons, didn't look at it that way. It was always extremist nationalist forces that stood behind such things regardless of who they -- whose -- who they belonged to. So separatists are the same all round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, since you said this, since you said this assessment was correct, did this second variant occur? Because on the 27th of June, 1991, there was a conflict between the Territorial Defence of Slovenia and the JNA, and about 50 unarmed soldiers of the JNA were killed and the Presidency of Slovenia assessed that it was the JNA that was the aggressor and they asked the population to organise resistance against them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is inaccurate what is being said in the media all the time, that these were unarmed soldiers, that these were children. They were armed like the entire JNA was armed. And the fact remains that the JNA was indeed proclaimed to be an occupying force, and that is the way it was treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the Presidency of Slovenia said that after this attack carried out by the Territorial Defence against the army, that the JNA was proclaimed the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've just said so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know exactly how many soldiers were killed in Slovenia at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a total of 56 members of the army lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that already three days later - this was on the 27th of June - on the 30th of June or the 1st of July, you were imprecise when you made a statement to the investigating judge in Belgrade in 1999. One unit of the JNA was attacked at the Mladost bridge in Zagreb when two members of the JNA were wounded. That is to say only three days after what had happened in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And then this blockade of the military barracks took place and everything that had to do with the military barracks, that was after that, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 30th of June, at the investigating judge's chambers in Belgrade, you said that an intercepted conversation between Alija Izetbegovic and Tudjman was recorded. On the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that day, the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in that intercepted conversation, Franjo Tudjman says to Alija Izetbegovic that it is time for Bosnia and Herzegovina to move against the JNA, and Alija Izetbegovic replied to him that he was following the situation but that it is not time to move yet. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the crisis in the work of the Presidency broke out only in March 1991, between the 12th and the 14th, when there was a four to four ratio within the vote in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, we've heard evidence about this, and this witness is merely going to give it secondhand. Given the constraints of time, I must ask you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm really trying to use up as little time as possible. Half an hour, 40 minutes. There is so much of this, Your Honours. I read that transcript for several months. This is a film of over 100 hours. I just tried to deal with the actual substance that was not dealt with until now. I'm making a maximum effort to bear time in mind, and I'll try to do that, but I would like you to view the situation in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question would be the following: You know that the first real foreign interference that took place was, and the General Staff was opposed to that, when Stipe Mesic took over as the president of the Presidency of the SFRY in the presence of the Troika of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from Mr. Mesic. We don't need this witness to go over that. If there's anything you can ask which he can deal with, of course you can ask it, but we don't need evidence to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. repeated. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I wish to ask Mr. Vasiljevic, and he knows about this for sure:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military leadership was opposed to that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opposed to what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Opposed to Mesic taking over that position in such a way.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military leadership did not interfere with the election of President Mesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you know that on the 20th of January, 1991, at the request of the government of Croatia, the Presidency of the SFRY allowed the extension of the deadline of -- for disbanding irregular units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that on the same day, Stipe Mesic, as vice-president to the Presidency of the SFRY stated before the parliament or, rather, at the Assembly of the HDZ that through various trading companies, the HDZ in Croatia bought weapons for themselves and that, therefore, the reserve police forces got the same powers as the regular police. In his opinion, the only paramilitary forces in Croatia were those in Kninska Krajina. That was on the same day or the following day after this decision of the Presidency was adopted, the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said quite literally, "Well, they didn't think that we are going to import pens in order to write requests to that effect."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, since the Presidency could no longer meet, that Stipe Mesic, without any decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, he did not have a relevant decision of the Presidency but, as Supreme Commander, he made public his decisions through the media but that he did not have any underlying decision of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know about their internal relationships.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to conclude all of this by saying one more thing that has to do with this. The international community, at one point in time, did it try to influence the Federal Secretariat for National Defence to take over the role of the Supreme Commander instead of the Presidency of Yugoslavia? And this was at a meeting held at the Federal Secretariat with Cyrus Vance at the end of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Veljko -- did Veljko Kadijevic tell you that it's best for the international community to do whatever they can in order for the Presidency to meet?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know about one particular case where an effort was made to exert some kind of pressure on the then commander of the air force to carry out a putsch and in this way reintroduce order in the country, because in the previous history of Yugoslavia, it was always the military that did that, but I'm not aware of any details of this conversation between the Federal Secretary and Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, I would like to conclude this particular topic by referring to the following: You know that the SSNO, the General Staff, and in the Supreme Command Staff nothing else was mentioned as an objective except preserving Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the military leadership did not pass a single decision or implement a single decision that was contrary to that objective?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more thing: Is it often said here in this courtroom, and perhaps you could explain this to the Judges, it is often said Belgrade, Belgrade, Belgrade had to be asked. Is it correct that the General Staff, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and the Supreme Command Staff had their headquarters in Belgrade, their seat in Belgrade, and that the Supreme Command Staff never went out into the field in their full composition?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could just briefly refer to Vukovar now, just a few brief questions related to Vukovar and Kosovo. I've dealt with this topic, I won't need more than about ten minutes for this. As regards Vukovar, Mr. Vasiljevic, do you know the exact number of members of the ZNG that were under siege in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us approximation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Vukovar, how many of them were in the town of Vukovar itself, I don't know. I know that they were reinforced all the time, that fresh forces were brought in, that the town had been prepared for a decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had fortified firing points in town on buildings, on residential buildings that they practically turned into bunkers. So their defence went from one building to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what form their armaments took? What kind of arms did they have?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some artillery weapons, they had some anti-aircraft light missiles, they had anti-armour equipment, rocket launchers and anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a film I got from the OTP, I saw that there were tanks as well that were taken away from the defenders of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The recording you saw was taken elsewhere. Ernestinovo or Lastovo, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said during the examination-in-chief that on the day you arrived in Vukovar, when the fighting subsided on the 19th of November, that on that day three soldiers were killed. You said that in response to Prosecutor Nice's question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there then, I was at Milici at a meeting with General Gracanin. That date is not correct. So the first time I came to Vukovar was perhaps a few days after the operation started when the Guards Brigade arrived, and then about 18 members of the military police were killed. There were wounded and killed persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers were killed in the fighting around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a total of 516.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the existence of an order that special attention should be devoted to prisoners in the following sense: That this will be very important for the exchange that should ensue, the exchange of prisoners? Wasn't there a telegram to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that taking prisoners was ever brought into the context of exchanges. Not that. But that the Geneva Conventions had to be applied and that all imprisoned persons had to be treated carefully. That certainly was a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see from the statement you gave to the investigating judge in Belgrade that you said that in your notebook, you wrote down that in Sremska Mitrovica there was a total of 1.300 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1.062, but possibly it was 1.300.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, but then in front of the KP Dom in Sremska Mitrovica, in buses at that time, there were an additional 1.050.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was this other figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, this other figure. And is it correct that you wrote down in your notebook that at one point in Sid there was a total of 5.000 prisoners and that then a very careful selection was carried out and that everybody that had nothing to do with the fighting in Vukovar were released, they could go wherever they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These 5.000 persons were not prisoners. These were 5.000 persons who got out of the town that was in ruins, and they were taken by the Red Cross of Serbia in Sid and Mitrovica and that is where people were asked as to where they wanted to go and whether they had anybody they could stay with and who could take care of them. So these were the two columns that the Croats did not allow to enter Croatia, although they wanted to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As regards prisoners of war, were two collection centres established in Stajicevo and Begejci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are centres of the 1st Military District, the 1st Army District, and they did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to what your notebook said, in Stajicevo there were 1.283 prisoners. On the 16th of December, 1991, you toured Stajicevo and Begejci, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you established that there were 1.324 prisoners in Stajicevo and 133 in Begejci.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that a certain number were identified as those who have committed the gravest crimes because in these centres that we referred to were seen by Red Cross teams four times before you went there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I heard from witness Dr. Bosanac that you were present in an aeroplane when an exchange was carried out of over 50 persons, that you were the person who carried this out.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another thing in this relation that I would like to ask you about. Any of these prisoners, any of these prisoners of war who were in these localities where they were, were any of them killed, to the best your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the case that was mentioned of a soldier, a reservist, Goran Nikolic, who had killed four persons. I presented that during my previous testimony. And I think that until the end there were eight cases of deaths. All of them were investigated and all of them had to do with natural death causes. However, the numbers from Stajicevo and Begejci should not be summed up and equalised to the number in Sremska Mitrovica, because when I came to the area, I was interested in seeing what this collection centre was, and it was my assessment that the conditions there were not right for accommodating these people because it was very cold and the facilities had no heating, and I intervened at the Supreme Command Staff with this particular bit of information. After that, they were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica and to the KP Dom in Nis where the conditions were quite normal for having them stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 80 were prosecuted but then ultimately there was an exchange all for all and no longer was any attention paid to who were suspects for what, and towards the end of 1992 there was ultimately an exchange?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August 1992 there was an exchange of all for all and about 800 persons to the best of my knowledge, and at that time I was in detention together with them, were exchanged for a total of 34 men. Most of them were civilians from the territory of Yugoslavia. Not a single person who was suspected of having committed a war crime - and there was a total of 186 of them in proceedings before the military court in Belgrade - not a single one of them was exchanged. So those who were suspects or who were already convicted of having committed war crimes were not involved in exchanges. Other people were being exchanged, those who had taken part in the armed rebellion but those who had not committed any crimes on their own. So therefore, these 50, if they were exchanged then, and I think that this was the 10th of December, 1991, they were exchanged for imprisoned members of the JNA from Gospic and some other pilots like Stojcinovic who had been kidnapped and others whose planes were downed. But none of them had the status of a criminal or a suspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that will be sufficient. We don't have time to go into details. Let me end with a few more questions regarding Kosovo. I think that you could know that immediately after the end of the Second World War, an order was issued that all those who had left Kosovo during the war, even if they had a home and land there could not return to Kosovo. Are you aware of that law? And it related in the first place to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of a law that was enacted immediately after the Second World War --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we've ruled that this sort of evidence is way out of our time span, particularly with this witness. It may be there will be an historian who can deal with those matters, but not this witness. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour. There will probably be other opportunities to hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you please tell us about the last 20 years or so, between the 1970s and the 1990s. At certain points in time were their crises, as with the Martinovic case, that triggered drastic emigration of Serbs from Kosovo? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such an event would occur that would trigger the Serbs moving out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to Martinovic, for instance, in 1985?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was physically mistreated. He was stripped naked and a beer bottle was pushed into his anus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this followed by massive departure from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This process of the moving out of Serbs was a continuous process, but an event of this kind, such as rapes, also would speed up this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to limit this questioning. You really must, Mr. Tapuskovic, deal with the time which this witness dealt with, which was 1999. If you want to ask him some questions about that, you can, but events back in history are not going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was not history. This was a process that continued for decades regarding Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is history. As far as we're concerned, it is. Now, move on. If you want to ask him something about 1999 and his evidence, you can, but asking general questions, you cannot. I've already explained, there will be an historian who can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will hear a witness who is due to come in the next few days who said that Mr. Vasiljevic was the person most knowledgeable about events in Kosovo, but of course I will abide by your ruling, Your Honour May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to know in 1989 and 1990 and the years you have testified about, those five or six years prior to 1990, was there a very pronounced emigration of Albanian citizens moving into the territory of Kosovo with their whole families and remaining there to live?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had emigrated from Albania under the Enver Hoxha regime were received as immigrants to Kosovo and were given homes and land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And allowed to live normally there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as is the case with all other immigrants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I think that will be sufficient. But as someone who went to Kosovo again in his official capacity in April 1999, did you then, while staying in Kosovo and doing the work you did, did you learn anything about what had happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You hadn't even heard what happened at Racak?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard earlier on from the media. There were opposing views about it, but I really didn't inquire about it, nor was there any private discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived, the NATO bombing was under way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point in time, was the most important, the priority, the top priority for the army and the civilian population to protect the army and the civilians regardless of their ethnicity? Wasn't that the dominant task of the army and the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is precisely the sort of issue we are going to have to deal with. The Trial Chamber is going to have to determine what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Vasiljevic had a very important job in the army, and I'm asking whether he knows that these were the main tasks of the army at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When ground -- there was a threat of ground forces intervening.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The emphasis was on securing the frontier area and anti-air defences because of the constant NATO raids and attacks on military facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the KLA take advantage of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were KLA groups in inaccessible areas, that they were surrounded and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of administrative matters. We will be serving an historian's report. We may have filed it already. Whether in the event this will be a witness for whom there will be enough time is a matter that I'm uncertain about. It's a matter I'm going to turn to next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we will need to make time for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Oh, it's a her. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's topic that I've got to discuss with you. As to Kadijevic's book, the practice in the past has been, I think, to exhibit the single page that has been referred to the witness. Mr. Tapuskovic referred to a number of pages to this witness. I've got a number that I might like to ask him about as well. It's quite a substantial book, but it may be easier, frankly, for the Chamber to have the whole book as an exhibit. Of course on the basis that it's merely what it is, a book, because others may want to delve into it as well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think in due course we will have to consider this, but for the moment we are bound by the witness's answers. It's his answers which is the evidence, not the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have quite a number of matters of re-examination. I'll try and deal with them in an orderly way. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just a couple of opening points and then I'll try and deal with things chronologically, but quite recently, you were distinguishing between Macedonia and Slovenia on the one hand and the other parts of the former Yugoslavia on the other when you were asked about the peaceful separation of Macedonia. You seem to be saying, correct me if I'm wrong, that the difference between those two states and the others were that there were no Serbs in Macedonia or in Slovenia. Is that what you understand to be the distinguishing feature as to why those states separately peacefully?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there were no Serbs, but I said that they did not constitute a significant number, and that is why in Macedonia or, rather, in Slovenia there were no plebiscites of Serbs or any referendums as to which state they wanted to live in. And that is why this problem of the withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia and Macedonia evolved far more easily. In Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, the Serbs at their referendum stated their will to live in Yugoslavia. The problem was that it was more or less accepted that they could live in Yugoslavia but that they should go to Yugoslavia to do that and not take the territory with them. And this contradiction actually led to armed conflict and a civil war subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another general point on this, and obviously a lot of questions, you've been there a long time, whenever you can answer a question briefly it would be in all our interests for you to do so. You made your comments about whether it was boys or soldiers that went from the JNA to Slovenia. You were in the army; if the army had wanted to take and retain Slovenia by force, could it have done so, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, without any doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last -- no. One more particular point: When you were dealing with your meetings with the accused in relation to Kosovo in 1999, the accused put a number of propositions to you about that meeting to suggest that what he was saying in the meeting was a reflection of a single reality, a reflection of his intentions, a reflection of how things were being done. Just yes or no, do you accept that what he was saying was the only version of events, the only version of reality, or may there have been other realities apart from what he was saying to you in that meeting? Just yes or no, please, a single word answer.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my own impressions. I cannot present reliable facts that there was something else in evidence which we in the military leadership did not have access to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already spoken of one or two characteristics of the meeting, who was there, who wasn't there, who remained afterwards, and so on. Just yes or no to this -- if you feel you can answer, just yes or no: Is there material available to you or known to you that assists in your consideration that there was another reality behind the accused's presentation? Were there other material that led to you thinking there was another reality? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again just yes or no: Is that material that you're able to refer to to this Chamber, either in open session or in closed session?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If in the course of my re-examination you wish to draw to their attention anything in that respect, perhaps you'll let us know. Kadijevic's book. Can I ask you for your comments on a few other passages. You've already said that his reference to the Karlobag line is one you don't acknowledge, understand or accept, I think. Page 49 of the book, he spoke of there being three phases for the tasks of the concept of deployment, saying that at the beginning of this phase, the armed force's task was to defend the Serb nation in Croatia and its national interest, the second was to pull the JNA garrisons out of Croatia, and third was to gain full control of Bosnia and Herzegovina, fourth was to create and defend new Yugoslav state of those Yugoslav nations that desired to be part of it. Do you accept that analysis of four objectives for deployment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that that is where I disagree with certain parts of the book, in view of the fact when that book was written by General Kadijevic and under which circumstances. This was the period when I was in prison. This was the period when I was interrogated, and I was told that if I open up and say what Kadijevic, Adzic, and Brovet were doing, I would fare better. So objectively, there was a climate in which Kadijevic was, in a strange way, given the facilities to be able to write this book. And later on, one could not obtain military information, even very ordinary information. So I think in those days he was writing things that people wanted to hear. I do not know that forces were deployed from Slovenia to Bosnia to control Bosnia. In Bosnia, there was sufficient forces. The question was where to deploy the forces from Slovenia. Some of them were deployed in Montenegro, in Bar, for instance. So I don't find this approach of General Kadijevic's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you just a couple more passages, because you've been asked extensively about it, but disagree as His Honour the Presiding Judge, Judge May has said, in a sense your disagreement is enough, but qualify it, of course, when you want to. Page 52, the General said: "The constants of the war in Croatia were that the Serb nation had to be defended, that is, liberated there where it lived." Do you accept that analysis of what happened in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a highly simplified analysis of the overall situation. It all depends which stage we're talking about. In the first stage, when there was massive arming on a party basis, that is the HDZ line, and when minimum quantities of arms were distributed and there was this demonstration of force around the areas mostly inhabited by Serbs, I spoke about these newly formed 19 police stations around the Serb inhabited areas, then such a statement would apply to that period, that there was fear and efforts were made for the people to organise themselves locally, by settlement, out of fear of incursion of those forces as they remembered they had done earlier on in history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps lastly, though I may conceivably come back to it, the last passage I would like your comment on at page 83, dealing with attacks that were made on the JNA, and I pause to just ask you a question: General, do you remain proud of the JNA of which you were a member, as a matter of fact and so that we can have your perspective?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am proud as an officer and any other senior officer who chose this profession of his own free will, and I am proud of having been a member of that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then Kadijevic said this of those who attacked the JNA, ignoring its positive accomplishments, especially for the new Yugoslavia and particularly for the Serb nation in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he went on to say: "At the same time, they hoped to compromise the policy of the current Serbian leadership which ran the JNA even before." So in writing, Kadijevic was speaking of the Serb leadership running the JNA. Do you disagree with that expression of his or do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree, because at meetings that I attended, even my critical attitude towards the Serbian leadership - and this was noted in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. my notebook, so I adopted a critical attitude - there were obstructions to the mobilisation, obstruction to assisting the armed force being rounded off properly, reinforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there must be a misunderstanding with the interpreters, because I see here on the transcript that the witness had a critical attitude towards the Serbian leadership, but I understood that the witness said he did not agree because meetings that he attended, Kadijevic had a critical attitude to the Serbian leadership. And this is a rather significant difference in relation to the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcript says otherwise. We will ask the witness to clarify. Was it yours or Kadijevic's attitude which was critical, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not my attitude but the attitude of General Kadijevic and other members of the military leadership that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now going to deal with things chronologically, please. I think you were asked some questions about agreements on -- involving the HDZ in perhaps March of 1990 about the JNA. Then in May you spoke of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, yes, what is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I quote a single piece of paper, you insist that the witness has to have it in front of him, and I feel he needs to have the book in front of him to be able to find the quotations and to be able to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The book isn't evidence. What's evidence, as I've said, is what the witness says about it. Now, I've allowed both Mr. Tapuskovic and Mr. Nice to put passages to the witness so he can comment on them. It's the comments which is the evidence, not what's in the book. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken, General, of JNA support for Serbs in Croatia facing, as you describe it, the difficulties of secession, and the Serbs were armed, including being the beneficiaries of arms released from places where they were stored. Whose authority and at what level was the authority given to release those arms to Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my earlier testimony, I always said that I did not agree with the expression "the arming of the Serbs by the JNA." Legal units of the Territorial Defence were formed, which hadn't existed in the area. I spoke about of the 6th Lika Division and other units which had their numerical markings and were subordinated to the JNA. And as far as I know, it was just a question of arming and completing those units of the Territorial Defence, whereas the expression "the arming of the Serbs" is being used as if they were a paramilitary structure, and I am not aware of that. I did speak of individual cases. I mentioned four such cases when some minor quantities of weapons were given or were prevented from being given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
