utterances.text: The question I'd still like your answer to, please, is this: If weapons were released to Serbs that had previously been stored on the territory, what level of authority would be required for that release?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think such a decision would have to come from the Presidency, and in operational terms, to be executed by the JNA. But I repeat, you keep using the term "arming of the Serbs." I'm talking about the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, to your knowledge, General, was the first Serb or representative of the Serb DB in, say, Knin? Can you help us with that? When abouts in 1990, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of the second half of 1990. I joined the security administration on the 8th of July, 1990, and then maybe I had my first information about this in the following two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Spegelj material, and I'm not going to ask you very much about that, was available at the end of 1990, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which material you're referring to, which specific material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The material from which you take direct responsibility, the films, the secret films which you say were definitely him, when did you have those first available to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first shots or audio recording was made on the 14th of October, 1990. The first TV recording was made on the 19th of October, 1990. And then successively from then on. That is as far as the recordings are concerned. As for knowledge, information as to what Spegelj was doing and what he was advocating, I've had that knowledge ever since the 2nd of October, 1990. And the chief of security in the 5th Military District some ten days before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence correctly that the material that you commissioned is material that you say unequivocally is Spegelj speaking, caught by the secret camera?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other material which has been cut into it or spliced into it is not material for which you take personal direct responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume I don't have direct responsibility for what I filmed secretly either, because I was discovering the preparation of an armed rebellion against Yugoslavia. If that was correctly interpreted to me. That's why I'm saying this. The other parts of the film came from public statements by the persons shown on those films.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the cutting of that material into the material you'd commissioned and the use of that other material cut into the material you commissioned was done by others, it wasn't done by you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I explained that in those days, I was mostly in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, unless I've got it wrong, you're not in a position to say definitively that that other material is always Spegelj's voice? I'm not saying it isn't, I'm just saying that you're not in a position to say definitely, always, for every sentence, it is his voice?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying emphatically and claiming that it is his voice, that I personally recorded those secret meetings that they held, that the material secretly filmed was throughout under my full control and that only a part of the material was provided for the film to be made and selecting that material and fitting it into the future film was something I attended, I was present there. And afterwards, the material was in my hands again. So there's absolutely no doubt that this is absolutely trustworthy material because I filmed it myself and I had it in my own possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may come back to that, but I doubt it. And one last question on Spegelj: Why, given the availability of the material in the autumn of 1990, was it not made available to the public until a date in the spring of 1991? What was the purpose served by that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of filming the material was not to make a film. We were working on the discovery of paramilitary organisation and illegal import of weapons and professionally provided appropriate documents for court proceedings and for stopping those activities. So the material wasn't made to make a film out of it. Now, why it was finally released on the 25th of January, it was because, up until that material was shown, the leaders of Croatia, from Franjo Tudjman through Stipe Mesic, denied that there was any illegal import of weapons in Croatia or the organisation of paramilitary organisations within the auspices of the HDZ. I wasn't in Belgrade when this was released, but I was reported -- I was informed about it. It was only once he saw the film that Tudjman changed his position and promised that the perpetrators would be handed over to the courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to aspects of control that you were asked about extensively, particularly in relation to the Territorial Defence. You told the learned Judges about the three states that could trigger a change in control; a state of emergency, imminent threat of war, state of war. By the beginning of 1991, had there been any relevant declaration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 1991. I can speak of 1981 and 1989, when states of emergency were proclaimed in Kosovo, but in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any such declaration of binding, lawful effect during 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you say that was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, as far as I can recollect, but I can't be absolutely certain of that, I think it was either at the end of September or the beginning of October when a state of imminent danger of war was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the Rump Presidency, without representatives of most of the former states?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, for us, it was the Presidency and that the position of the military leadership was that even if one member of that Presidency is operating and the others are not prohibited from attending, we would treat them as the Supreme Command. The Presidency, such as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is now 12.15. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, General, the Territorial Defence in Eastern Slavonia, you were asked questions by the accused challenging you as to whether you were right to describe there being two types of Territorial Defence, and at one stage you said to him on day one, on the 13th of February, last Thursday, "I was explaining about the Territorial Defence headed by people from your MUP." I don't know if that's something you feel you can particularise in any greater detail in open or closed session.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have discussed this at great length. I have nothing to add to what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this relate to the man Badza?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown a list of, or read out, I can't remember which, a list of 16 generals for the year 1991, and you regularly tried to distinguish between what happened at the beginning and the end of 1991, I'm not sure that you ever finally got the answer out. First of all, we can check it if necessary, but did that 16 -- did those 16 generals include, I think, some four who were in charge of things like academies rather than in charge of fighting units? The exhibit is D101, but I don't want to take time looking at it. It doesn't matter if you can't remember. I'm not going to take the time on that. But what was the change during the first and second half of 1991 that you wanted to draw to our attention as to the composition of generals by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the accused claimed insistently that in 1991, there were only two Serbs, maybe three, who were in the general -- who were among the generals. And I said that until June 1991 and after that, in 1991 there were shifts in posts and retirement of certain generals, and I named names and posts. Which of them were academicians, I didn't check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that changed, did it change the ethnic balance or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the generals are concerned and people in command functions, there were changes, specifically in the 1st Military District, in the 2nd Operative Group. The commander was replaced and also all the other persons I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hadzic appointing Territorial Defence in Eastern Slavonia, if he did in his role as Prime Minister or president of the body there, so far as you were concerned, to whom did he answer, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he was appointing, and I don't know to whom he answered, if he did. I stand by what I said, namely that the most influential man in that area, including personnel affairs and the use of those units, of what I called the 2nd Territorial Defence was Badza Stojicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so as far as you could see, there was no formal line of reporting to an official government body or to a minister or anything of that sort, apart from what you've described?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that line, and I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your capacity in 1991, you would obviously have been concerned about any reports of wrongdoings. Before we look at them, just tell us this: If there were amnesty reports, Amnesty International reports, on Serbian paramilitary forces' wrongdoing, would they have come to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attention?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was supposed to have shown them to me, who had these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally in your position there and knowing what you did in the government, if international humanitarian organisations were preparing reports in the autumn of 1991 complaining of, for example, Serbian paramilitary wrongdoing, should that have been made available to you by your government, for example?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not subordinated to any government, I was subordinated to the Federal Secretary for National Defence, and I believe that considering the department I belonged to, I don't think that report would have come to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom should such reports have gone, then, and we'll move on, but to whom should such reports have gone assuming they were handled by the government at all or the military at all? Who should have had them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a foreign non-governmental organisation, and I don't know to whom, if anyone, they sent their reports. I don't know that any such reports reached me or the top leadership of the military at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't take the time of the Court by showing them to the witness, but it will help us just then to have this picture, General: In the time until your dismissal in 1992 and at your level of the army, are you saying that no regard was being taken, to your knowledge, of international reporting on wrongdoing by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA, within its system, did not monitor such things. I suppose that in the federal government, there was a service dealing with the writings of foreign media, but there was no such institution in the army. Such things did not reach us. We were not given such things for consideration and review.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Neither the federal government nor the government of Serbia disseminated this information to the army, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not so far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Matters of detail, you were asked questions this morning about Lovas again and Teslic. You gave a very detailed answer to His Honour about to whom you reported when there was confusion in the questioning of the accused. Should we be distinguishing between Lovas and Teslic, and should we be distinguishing as to whom you informed about each?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distinction should be made, because as far as Lovas is concerned, I was then in active service and my job was such that I had to send information on. As far as Teslic is concerned, I was not in active service and the knowledge I gained was indirect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to your -- no. That was in closed session, I won't trouble with it. I'll move on. There was a suggestion at some stage that -- by the accused, that paramilitaries at this time were being created only by opposition parties. Do you accept that or not? And then I have a supplementary question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. I don't know that the party in power then set up any paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then when we look at the parties that were setting them up, were the goals of those parties, although technically opposition, themselves sympathetic to the objectives of the accused?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say that for certain. At that time, I thought, and I still believe, that the creation of those paramilitary units was aimed primarily at creating some sort of political image, that these parties were fighting for the interests of those Serbs who were in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If such paramilitary units were established, do you know - and if not, we can have a look at the relevant article - what would be the consequence under the All People's Defence law of 1982 for their control? Do you know if they were to be considered part of the armed forces generally?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a procedure according to which units are formed as an integral part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just have a look, please, at one part, for your comment, at the All People's Defence law of 1982. Thank you very much. It's already been tendered as Exhibit 352, tab 21. If we can just lay this on the overhead projector, if you get a chance. English for the overhead projector and original for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just looking at Article 91 of the All People's Defence law for 1982, which reads: "The armed forces make up a single entity and are comprised of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, any citizen who with weapons or in any other fashion participates in resistance against the enemy is also considered a member of the armed forces." The paramilitary groups that you've been asked to talk about and have spoken of having some political impetus behind them, should they not qualify, or should they qualify for being considered a member of the armed forces under this law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just one article that deals with the issue of who may become part of the armed forces. But there are mechanisms according to which they have to be organised in terms of uniform, emblems, line of command, and all the other elements that make up the armed forces regardless of whether we're talking about the Territorial Defence or the Yugoslav People's Army. And such groups, some of which I mentioned, did exist outside the system. And there was an order regarding recruitment of these volunteers into the legal units of the armed forces. And I'm now talking about the JNA and the Territorial Defence, both. So it is not enough for someone to be armed to become a member of the armed forces. There are other attributes, other standards that have to be met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that they were all incorporated into the armed forces or are you saying that in some way they were allowed to operate outside control?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said neither of these things. I said that by interpreting only this first article, Article 91 that you quoted, it is not the only attribute that someone has to have in order to become a member of the armed forces, to be armed. I know of some groups that came from certain political parties in the Knin Krajina who were expelled from there. They were returned by the same bus in which they arrived. These groups were backed and organised mainly by the political party of the SPO, Serbian Renewal Movement. And I spoke about cases concerning the centres for admission of volunteers organised by the JNA in 1991 when people didn't want to put on their JNA uniform or wear its emblems and were removed from these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very briefly, one other exhibit already tendered, part of 352, tab 24, please, which is the Official Gazette for the Republic of Serbia's decree on proclamation of defence law. We only need look at the first two sides of that. I'm sorry there's so much of it. There's only the first sheet, in fact, Your Honours. I'm sorry I've caused so much to be copied. I should have reduced it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see that this decree on proclamation of defence law of the Republic of Serbia in the Gazette, dated the 27th of July of 1991 has - and, Your Honour, it's on the second page, article -- beg your pardon. It's way in. Article 118. If you would go to Article 118, General, please. It says here, apparently clearly, that "Only competent state bodies may organise, reinforce, arm, equip, and train armed forces." Were you aware of that provision? And how would that fit with the existence on the territory of paramilitary groups apparently outside the system?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have previous opportunity to see this article or this Official Gazette of Serbia, for that matter. I think that this is completely appropriate in terms of who may organise and reinforce. That should only be a competent state authority. This probably means the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, because this is the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A couple of questions about Vukovar. I took you only to a very limited part of what your inquiry had revealed when you asked questions of Vukovar. The accused asked you rather more. Can you help us, please: When you sought information from Sljivancanin and Mrksic, had they already been indicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were, because I said in which years it happened. I met with Sljivancanin in 1997 and with Mrksic in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, have you seen the evacuation agreement that existed at the time, that we've seen recently as an exhibit in this case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which evacuation you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the hospital. Have you seen that one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that was an agreement in full or in good order providing for a proper and orderly evacuation. You've been asked about the JNA's involvement or non-involvement in all this. If the JNA had custody of those men who were subsequently killed, slaughtered. Would they need authority to hand them over to some other body, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume they would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think part of the account that was given in the circumstances you've confirmed for us was that Sljivancanin was worried by the local Territorial Defence, but in your experience, the JNA would be a match for the local Territorial Defence, would it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local Territorial Defence was no match for the JNA. However, the people who made it up were capable of uncontrolled acts. So it's not a question of the balance of power between the Territorial Defence and the JNA, it was the climate in which it happened, where people from the local Territorial Defence acted in the way which I testified about, as well as other witnesses. So there was a danger to the people involved from the part of the extremists in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction. The witness is talking about individuals from the Territorial Defence and the acts of the individuals from the Territorial Defence, whereas there is no mention of that in the interpretation, it just says Territorial Defence. The witness said clearly "individuals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two more questions, General.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two more questions, General. Are you aware of regulations on the application of international laws of war on the armed forces of the SFRY dated 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I am aware of these regulations and laws, but I don't know which specific law you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would they cover the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to my first question and just to see if we're quite clear, for the JNA to release a large number of men in their custody and control to another body would require authority from someone or other if it was to be done properly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there existed an agreement between the competent authorities of Croatia about exchanges of prisoners of war and detained persons, and there was a special body, organ in the JNA which dealt with these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're concerned, you understand, with releasing of men in circumstances that they got slaughtered in the way we know about. For them to be released by the JNA, some authority would have to be given, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to be speaking about prisoners of war and exchanges. As far as I know, there was no exchange in Vukovar. Exchanges took place later, up until August 1993 -- sorry, 1992. And if we are talking about people who were taken prisoner from the hospital in Vukovar, there was no exchange there. They were turned over under the circumstances that I witnessed and that I described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't take that any further. Dubrovnik. You seemed to give slightly contradictory answers at one stage as to whether there had been actions mounted from Dubrovnik. You spoke of forces coming across the Neretva River, which could be many kilometres away from Dubrovnik, and then at another stage you seemed to answer the accused that there had been some action coming out of Dubrovnik. Can you just clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I said that the forces of the ZNG from the area of Western Herzegovina, and I know specifically about Metkovici, were transferred to Dubrovnik through a part of the Bosnian territory, namely the municipality of Neum, and they acted from Dubrovnik. So that is the context in which I spoke. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just break this down because the Judges may be very interested in this: When you say "from Dubrovnik," are you suggesting the old town, the fortress, or the surrounding area, the wider part of Dubrovnik, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a commander in this area, nor did I go to that area in the time concerned, but based on the information that reached me, meaning news, I knew that there were actions from the old part of the town and from Dubrovnik as a whole. And I spoke about the simulation of destruction that was carried out by setting on fire old tyres. But this is sporadic knowledge that I gained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's knowledge that you received from others. For example, the car tyres, was it car tyres or was it cars on fire, their tyres also being on fire, which we've seen in -- or the results of which we've seen in video footage, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only know about the information that tyres were set on fire, and it's not that I know that cars were on fire and that the smoke came from those car tyres. So it meant that there was this kind of arson in order to alarm the international public. That's the information that I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But none of it firsthand or secondhand; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in that area. This came from the security organs, from the 2nd Operative Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this comment is wrong, because the witness is testifying in view of his position as chief of the security administration of the military. He is testifying about what he had within the official information he received from official organs, and now firsthand or secondhand does not really amount to much in this particular context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will have to decide what weight to give to the in evidence due course. Anything more?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on Dubrovnik, when do you say the JNA was threatened from Dubrovnik? Where was the JNA when it was threatened and when was it threatened, on the intelligence that you received?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that first and foremost I was not head of the intelligence administration. And secondly, this is not an area that the security organs dealt with. I do not have reports that arrive regularly, and the task of the security organs is not to report from that area how military operations were being carried out. So I did not have this kind of information. This was through contacts with security organs that had to do with completely different professional issues, and it was only to the extent to which I've already referred to. So I cannot give reliable indicators in this regard because I was not in charge of that, according to my own line of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 1992. Now, you were -- in chief, General, you didn't provide any evidence about Bosnia. You effectively were out of office by then, and it may be that you expressed a view about whether you really wanted to give bits of evidence about Bosnia, given that history. But you've been asked a number of questions, and I'll just ask you a few arising from them. In fact, the VRS and the SVK, who paid for them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that at that time, I was retired. I spoke clearly about the financing. As for personal incomes, salaries, officers for the, officers in the army of Republika Srpska, I've already explained that, and I really have nothing to add to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, there's been various suggestions about the true separateness of these various forces. Was there any source of funding that you were aware of, because you had your contacts - and you've been asked questions about this by the accused, you see - was there any source of funding for the VRS other than that which came from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say the VRS, you are probably referring to the period after 1992. As regards that period, I haven't got any facts. I talked about part of the funding that went through in 1991 when I met with that man who participated in the transfer of money. But that was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if you'd look at one document for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a new exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 388. And the document, so we have it for the record, the document of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, dated 14 October 1992, will be marked for identification as Defence Exhibit 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, what I'm asking you to look at is a decision of the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the session held on the 14th of May of 1992, which is just after you -- literally days after you were pensioned off if we've got the record accurate. And the decision reads -- the decision on using primary issue funds, and it says this: "Primary issue --" which I take to be the printing of money -- "of the National Bank of Yugoslavia will be used in accordance with the National Bank of Yugoslavia decision on goals and tasks of common monetary policy and common principles of credit policy ..." And: "In order to avoid adverse effects of the war on the economy of the Serbian Republic, up to ... 80 per cent of primary issue will be used for special purposes." They will be transferred to special purpose accounts. Do you know what was meant by that? And I'd like to show you one other document as well, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think again, Your Honour, this will be a new document. And while we're finding it, I'm sorry to -- I apologise to Ms. Dicklich for not having given her earlier notice of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I'm not aware of this at all. And anyway, I'm not an expert in that particular field, the field of finance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, General. But in light of the questions that have been asked about the nature of these forces and their suggested separateness, and in light of your contact with -- maintaining of contact with highly placed people into the period of the Bosnian conflict, I'd like your answer on the next document and one other document that I'll refer to. This next document --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that I'm missing something, because I got this decision. This is the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska and the decision on the use of funds, and the registrar said that this exhibit has to do with that and with some other document of the JNA. I don't have any JNA documents here within this exhibit. As far as I can see from the transcript, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The JNA document was the one which you produced and has been exhibited amongst the Defence exhibits. So there's been a -- there have been these -- wait a moment. There have been these documents which are produced now, and also the JNA document is one of your exhibits, marked for identification. Mr. Nice, I wonder if we're really straying rather far from this witness's evidence here. There's a limit to what he can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but he was used as a vehicle for a number of assertions by the accused aimed at suggesting separateness of these various bodies and independence from the accused. The witness was relied on for his proximity to sources -- to positions of power for the answers that he gave, and with this exhibit, which is a small exhibit, and with one other reference that I will explain in a minute, I'll invite his comment, if I may. It won't take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to finish the witness by quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is a document, Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska, requesting credit for primary emission in Yugoslav dollars -- dinars, and it says in the second paragraph: "It is known that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has approved certain means from the primary emission for the needs of the Republika Srpska and that the realisation is handled by the Komercijalna Banka from Belgrade," and then there is a reference to a particular supplier. So that that again refers to money coming from the Yugoslav bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I was going to ask the witness to have that in mind and also to have a paragraph from the factual basis for the plea of guilty of Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I think we'll need to think very carefully before that is put in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I -- can I be heard on that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a document by -- that we're going to say is an admissible document in any event at some stage, subject to other evidential sources of similar materials overtaking events. It's a public document and it constitutes a fully acknowledged statement of an individual. Witnesses throughout this trial are commenting on statements, whether in books or in more formal settings of other individuals not immediately present, and in our respectful submission, it would be unrealistic not to take account of what has been said in the particular circumstances by that individual. It's paragraph 14 on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, it is much too early to put that sort of document in. I agree that we have allowed witnesses to comment on documents, but this is a much more controversial one in the circumstances of this case, and I would not be happy about it being put to a witness, I have to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt you could make the point shortly, and if you wish to produce other evidence, of course you can in due course, but it doesn't seem to me to be right through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I shan't take time any further on it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems to us that we're getting a very long way from the evidence that this witness can usefully give, and he's being used as a vehicle for comment that in any circumstance really would not be helpful for the Trial Chamber, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Nice, we are a Tribunal of professional Judges. We are not a jury. And we have heard what the witness has said. We know what the limit of his expertise is. These documents, of course it's open for you to put in front of us, but I don't think we need these points argued, if I may say respectfully, through the witness when they can be argued by way of comment to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'm very happy to deal with it on that basis, and I'm only making the point through the witness because of the way he's been used on a topic that we didn't cover with him because of his own concerns. And if I can conclude this passage with one question, I'll move on. And the question is, in case the Court doesn't want it to be asked to the witness, whether he's aware of any other method of funding at the time for this army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course you can ask that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, were you aware of any other method of funding, apart from those pointed to in these documents, to the VRS other than those identified?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, apart from what I've been saying until now. And these are really rather specific questions. And even if I had been in active service, I wouldn't have had anything in common with these particular subjects and this particular subject matter. Apart from what I've testified to until now, I really have nothing else to add to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want the last document exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it can probably come in later through another witness because this witness has hardly dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move, because of the pressure of time, to the second phase of the -- and I'm going to rely on the fact that the witness's evidence on Bosnia was taken in the way it was and without examination-in-chief, and I'll come to the second phase of his evidence, which relates to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, General, you made a number of observations about the history of the Kosovo conflict which the Trial Chamber has indicated it is not interested in having in detail before it, certainly from you, without disrespect. I am going to ask you about one other report of a humanitarian kind which we have heard was distributed to the authorities. It's a report of Human Rights Watch which was Exhibit 198 and is already in evidence and is a report called "A Week of Terror in Drenica." Now, in your answers to the accused, you have said little or nothing of any wrongs done to the Kosovo Albanians, and the evidence before the Chamber is that this report, which falls within the period of time when you were in office just about, was made available in detail to the Serbian -- to the FRY, in fact, in various locations. Now, you may not have seen this document or you may have done - but if we look at the summary, Your Honour, and that's all we need to do to remind ourselves - this is a report that speaks of serious violations of international humanitarian law committed by Serbian and Yugoslav government forces in Kosovo's Drenica region in the last week of 1998, and goes on to deal with Racak. And what I want to know, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems to me we really should establish whether he knows of the document first of all before we ask him questions of a general nature. It is important whether he does know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly the question I'm going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can be asked whether or not he knows about the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. incidents which are described in the document. He must be entitled to give evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He can do that, but it seemed it was being said that he didn't want to ask that question, whether he'd seen it or not, according to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said you may not have seen the actual document. But first, have you seen the document? If not, was it or its general nature drawn to your attention by others?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this document. I'm not aware of its contents at all. And as regards the crimes that were committed in Kosovo, I have nothing to add to what I've already presented in my evidence. That is what I spoke about already. Racak did not occur while I was in active service, and I don't know at all about the details of what took place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, this question: If there is a report, and as I say it's in evidence that it was provided, detailing humanitarian or alleged humanitarian offences committed over the period September 1998 until March or so on of 1999, were the systems in place to which you were responding such that they were not drawn to your attention by a higher authority?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the interpretation I received is correct, you are asking me about something that took place while I was not in active service. So I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report relates to events either very shortly or comparatively shortly before you were in active service and alleges crimes of a grave kind that could be investigated. I want to know, please, whether the systems that were in place and of which you have spoken in dealing with the accused's questions, whether the systems in place did not allow for you to read such material.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There would have been no bans in terms of reading it or even checking out some of the information involved. I talked to you about the case of the journalist who published in foreign media information that was highly alarming. Immediately after that, we started checking out that information. But I do not know that this material was provided to the military organs, and I'm not aware of this at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One question on the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's -- in the original Prosecution exhibit binder - I'll just get the number - Exhibit 387, we did not look, because I was trying to save time, at a substantial document, tab 38. Thank you very much. If we could look at that with the witness. Only a couple pages of it need to be viewed, but in light of the questions asked by the accused, it's now material that we should look at this and not just take the witness's evidence on the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is the minutes or these are the minutes of something called the Joint Command, and we can see on the second side of the first page, over the page, it's for the 22nd of July of 1998, so it's before your period of interest, but nevertheless you've reviewed this document. And if the Court and the usher would be good enough first to go to page 27 of 164 and view that on the overhead projector. There's a passage. I'll have to read it to you, General, because I know you reviewed it and will probably notwithstanding the time you've been in the witness box be able to remember it. It's a passage which has Mr. Sainovic speaking of two detachments on -- it's just above the bit on the -- just down a tiny little bit. Usher, could you move it down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry, General. We're pressing for time. I'll read it to you. Mr. Sainovic was referring to - it's very short - two detachments on Mount Rudnik are to attack Lausa. The BG battle group must also be active in order to cut off Lausa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember that passage and its being in the minutes, what does that say to you about Sainovic's authority?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His authority was the commander of the Joint Command and to coordinate the operations of the MUP forces and the forces of the army of Yugoslavia with regard to a concrete assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. It's only want of time. If we go to page 50 of 164, please. While the usher is finding it to view, this is a passage where, General, Mr. Sainovic said this: "In the border belt, the army is to look at its obligations. In this area, the police are to cover all the territory and consolidate. DB are to cover and take over the third area." And then it ends with: "The DB and the army to make joint proposal for further plans."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 50 of 164, at the bottom of the page. Further down, Usher, please. That's it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember this passage, General, does this again accord with your explanation of the true function of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not look at these materials in such detail. They were only shown to me as minutes. I said then that I did not observe at the meeting that I attended on the 1st of June that anybody kept any kind of minutes. It is interesting to note here how, after these positions were presented by Mr. Sainovic, in view of the office that he held, how the commander of the military unit who was present at that meeting reacted. Now, did he inform the superior commander or command about this, and did he get verification for that? I don't know about that. I can only draw conclusions on the basis of what I saw and heard in my very own presence. The meeting ended simply with agreeing to what had been proposed, namely that what had been proposed should be done on the following day. And after that, the meeting was over. As for how the further mechanism went on, I do not know about that in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last passage which may help. Page 130 of 164, please. Bottom half of the page. The Chamber will recall the questions about the Joint Command and the Supreme Command, and here we can see Mr. Minic speaking of a preparation of a report concerning the realisation of the plan destroying DTS, measures, forces, instruments, results and consequences have to be presented. The headquarters has to write this report. And then it says this: "With this report, we have to go to the Supreme Command." Does this, General, if it's an accurate minute of the meeting, reflect what you understand about a connection between the Joint Command and the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that the Supreme Command should be informed about the reports that these commands to which this pertains should report on and that this should be given to the Supreme Command after the Joint Command deals with it. That was my understanding of it, if I understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last questions, about two or three of them and that's all, General - I'm sorry you've been detained so long - concern the meeting where missing people or killed people were dealt with, and you also made some reference to people being forced out of Kosovo. It will, of course, be for the Judges in due course to decide on what the evidence about figures reveals, and you've been asked questions, though, by the accused on these topics, but if there is evidence of some 800.000-odd people being compelled to leave Kosovo, and if there are exhumation figures totalling some 3.500 and more people killed in the crisis, is there any comment you can make which explains the gap between the much, much more modest figures you were dealing with and this scale of figure that the Judges may have to deal with in due course?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of the figures involved in Kosovo. I know about the killed and wounded members of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the army of Yugoslavia, rather. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at headquarters, I did not receive any information, any figures that would point to me that a policy of expelling Albanians from Kosovo was being pursued. I confined myself to my own area of work and my own line of work but I believe that nothing similar was taking place within the military leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And equally, so far as bodies exhumed in Serbia that may be traceable as bodies coming from Kosovo is concerned, some connected by DNA analysis to particular villages, do you have anything that you can help us with about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, General, I have a question. I'll be very brief. It's about the Vojna Linija and the police. Although the definition of Vojna Linija was dealt with in the open session, I think we'd better go into private session for safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- your time in private session after the witness has withdrawn, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're in open session. General Vasiljevic, that concludes your evidence. I'm sorry that you have been detained here as long as you have to give it, but thank you for coming. You are now free to go. If you'd like to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
